sentences: The heady early months of the startup ended with the first payroll they nearly missed.
Heady praise from a stranger is more dangerous than criticism from a friend.
Nobody hearkened to the engineer, who had been right in 1998 as well.
The phrase "hearken back" preserves a verb that otherwise died two centuries ago.
He hectored the witness until the judge intervened on the witness's behalf.
Homer's Hector was the hero; the verb, unfairly, remembers only his menace.

hedge.definition: to avoid committing; to limit risk
sentences: He hedged so thoroughly that both sides quoted him as an ally.
The fund hedged its position and lost less than everyone who had been certain.

hedonism.definition: devotion to pleasure as the highest good
sentences: The city's reputation for hedonism outlasted the clubs that earned it.
Philosophical hedonism is more disciplined than the holiday brochure version.
He called himself a hedonist and went to bed at ten every night.
The hedonist's problem is that pleasure requires increasingly expensive maintenance.
Had anyone heeded the second memo, there would have been no third one.
Heed the small warning and you rarely meet the large one.

hegemony.definition: dominance of one group over others
sentences: Naval hegemony bought a century of trade terms nobody else could refuse.
Cultural hegemony works best when it is mistaken for common sense.
Cleaning the archive was a herculean task and, like the labors, mostly unwitnessed.
Hercules had twelve labors; the intern had a filing cabinet.

heretic.definition: one who dissents from accepted belief
sentences: The heretic of one century is the syllabus of the next.
He was treated as a heretic for suggesting the data be published.
The heretical suggestion that meetings could be shorter was never raised again.
Heretical ideas travel fastest where they are most forbidden.

hermetic.definition: airtight; sealed off from outside influence
sentences: The hermetic world of the department admitted no outside evidence for twenty years.
Hermetically sealed jars and hermetically sealed disciplines both eventually spoil.
He built a hermitage at the end of the garden and called it an office.
The hermitage held one bed, one book, and forty years of silence.
Her heterodox methods produced results the orthodox ones had missed entirely.
Heterodox means other-teaching; orthodox means straight-teaching. Both are claims, not verdicts.
A heterogeneous committee argues more and decides better.
The sample was heterogeneous, which made the average meaningless.

hew.definition: to cut with blows; to adhere to closely
sentences: The steps were hewn from the rock by people whose names went unrecorded.
He hewed to the party line until the party changed it.
In its heyday the mill employed half the town and named the other half's streets.
Every heyday is identified only after it is over.
The hierarchical structure was drawn on one page and ignored on all the others.
Hierarchical organizations are efficient at obeying and terrible at noticing.
The formal hierarchy was on the wall; the real one met for coffee at eleven.
Every flat organization grows a hierarchy within eighteen months.
Bureaucracy hindered the rescue more effectively than the weather did.
Do not hinder someone doing your job for you.

hireling.definition: someone who works purely for pay
sentences: The hirelings did exactly what was contracted and not one minute more.
Calling an employee a hireling says more about the employer.
The histrionic resignation letter was leaked, framed, and quoted for years.
Histrionic grief at a public funeral raises questions no one is allowed to ask.

hoary.definition: old and stale; grey with age
sentences: He opened with a hoary joke that the audience had heard from his predecessor.
Hoary frost and hoary jokes share the same whiteness of age.
Sanctions hobbled the industry without ever quite closing it.
He hobbled to the finish line and refused a wheelchair on principle.
The regulation is a hodgepodge of three eras and four compromises.
Dinner was a hodgepodge of leftovers and, unexpectedly, excellent.
The film pays homage to four directors and steals openly from a fifth.
Homage was once a formal oath of loyalty; now it is a knowing camera angle.
His homespun wisdom charmed voters and alarmed economists.
The homespun aesthetic of the campaign cost four hundred thousand to produce.
The staff meeting ended with a homily about ownership that owned nothing.
A good homily is six minutes long; almost none are.
A homogeneous team agrees quickly and misses the same things together.
Milk is homogenized so the cream stops separating, which is a fair metaphor.
The neighborhood is architecturally homogenous and socially anything but.
Homogenous is technically a biology term that has swallowed homogeneous whole.
Investors were hoodwinked by a prospectus that mentioned the risk in a footnote.
To hoodwink was to blindfold someone before robbing them, which is honest etymology.
A horde of tourists arrived at eleven and the village disappeared until three.
Horde comes from a Mongol word for camp, which the camps earned.
The claim was hotly denied and quietly settled.
Two candidates hotly contested a seat that was abolished the following year.
Reporters hounded the family for a comment that never came.
He was hounded out of the job by a campaign nobody would admit to running.

hubbub.definition: a loud confused noise or commotion
sentences: The hubbub in the corridor made it clear the decision had leaked.
After the hubbub died down, the actual policy remained entirely unchanged.
It was hubris to name the ship unsinkable and hubris to sail it fast through ice.
Greek tragedy runs on hubris the way engines run on fuel.

humble.definition: to lower in pride or status
sentences: The result humbled a team that had spent the week explaining why it would win.
Nothing humbles a writer like reading their own first draft aloud.
The humdrum work of checking references is what keeps the exciting work honest.
He escaped a humdrum job for an exciting one and missed the humdrum one by March.
Correcting him publicly humiliated him and fixed nothing.
The scoreline humiliated a side that had been favorites for a decade.
They pitched the tent on a hummock and stayed dry while the field flooded.
Every hummock in that field marks a building nobody living has seen.
The trolley hurtled down the ramp and into a display of very expensive glass.
The deadline hurtled toward them at the usual, unstoppable rate.
She husbanded her energy through the first four rounds and won the fifth.
The estate husbanded its timber for two centuries and sold it in one.

husbandry.definition: careful management of resources or farming
sentences: Good husbandry kept the farm solvent through two droughts and one bank.
Financial husbandry is the least glamorous and most effective form of strategy.
"I've told you a million times" is hyperbole, and it has been said about that often.
Advertising is hyperbole with a legal department.
The coverage grew hysterical while the actual risk stayed unchanged.
Hysterical comes from the Greek for womb, which is a whole chapter of medical history.
The iconoclast of 1975 was giving keynote addresses by 1995.
Iconoclasts literally smashed images; now they merely smash assumptions on podcasts.
His iconoclastic first book made his name and his second one apologized for it.
Iconoclastic design ages faster than the conventions it mocked.

ideological.definition: based on a system of beliefs
sentences: The objection was ideological, which meant no amount of data would settle it.
Ideological purity and electoral arithmetic rarely share a room.

ideology.definition: a system of beliefs guiding action
sentences: An ideology explains everything, which is precisely the problem with it.
The party had an ideology at founding and a marketing department by year ten.
His one idiosyncrasy was writing every draft in green ink.
Idiosyncrasies are charming in a colleague and unbearable in a housemate.
Her idiosyncratic filing system was unusable by anyone else and flawless for her.
An idiosyncratic style is only called a style once it succeeds.
The idolatrous devotion of his fans made honest criticism impossible.
An idolatrous attitude to founders has killed more companies than competition.
The idolatry of growth crowded out every other measure of success.
Idolatry of the past is called heritage; idolatry of the future is called vision.
The idyllic photograph omits the motorway forty meters to the left.
Two idyllic weeks were followed by a bill nobody had discussed.
An ignoble motive can still produce a useful outcome, which complicates the moral.
It was an ignoble end to a career of genuine service.
The ignominious exit involved a taxi, a cardboard box, and a security escort.
An ignominious defeat is remembered longer than a narrow one.
He suffered the ignominy of being escorted from a building he had designed.
Ignominy fades; the photograph of it does not.
The illiberality of the committee showed in what it refused to discuss.
Illiberality with money is stinginess; with ideas it is worse.
The illicit trade moved through the same ports as the legal one and paid better.
Illicit is forbidden; elicit is drawing out. Confusing them creates strange sentences.
The gains were illusory: the currency had moved and nothing else had.
Illusory progress is more dangerous than none, because it stops the search.
An illustrious career ended over a dispute about a parking permit.
Illustrious predecessors make a difficult inheritance.
He imbibed the assumptions of the field before he could name any of them.
They imbibed rather more than intended and agreed to everything by midnight.
The whole imbroglio began with a misfiled expense claim for eleven pounds.
An imbroglio is a scandal that is too complicated to summarize.
The teacher imbued a whole generation with a suspicion of easy answers.
The room was imbued with the smell of coffee and old paper.
His immaculate record was the reason the accusation caused such disbelief.
The workshop was immaculate, which told you something about how little was built there.
Whether he liked the policy is immaterial; he signed it.
The objection was immaterial and consumed forty minutes anyway.
The collapse was imminent for three years before it finally arrived.
Imminent is about to happen, eminent is distinguished, immanent is dwelling within.

immure.definition: to shut away as if in prison
sentences: He immured himself in the library for a winter and emerged with the manuscript.
The word contains "wall": to immure is to build one around someone.
The laws of physics are immutable; the interpretations are revised annually.
Nothing in the contract was immutable except the fee.
Four hours of sleep impairs judgment as much as a legal limit of alcohol.
The injury impaired his grip and not, notably, his ambition.
The best teachers impart a method rather than a set of facts.
A drop of vanilla imparts more than its size suggests.
An impartial chair is worth two clever ones.
He claimed to be impartial and was seen dining with one side twice.

impasse.definition: a deadlock with no way forward
sentences: The talks reached an impasse over a word that appeared once in an annex.
An impasse is broken by a new fact or a new person, rarely by a new argument.
He remained impassive through the verdict and wept in the corridor.
The impassive face of the negotiator was the most valuable thing in the room.
Her timing was impeccable, arriving exactly as the objection was being formed.
Impeccable literally means incapable of sin, which is a lot to ask of a haircut.
The impecunious student ate the same meal for a year and learned to cook it well.
Impecunious poets are a cliché that the rent has kept remarkably accurate.
Roadworks impeded the ambulance for four crucial minutes.
The Latin root is "in the feet": to impede is to shackle.
The only impediment to the plan was that it required money nobody had.
A speech impediment ended his broadcasting career and started a better one in print.

impel.definition: to drive or urge into action
sentences: Curiosity impelled her to open a file that had been sealed for forty years.
Impel pushes from behind; compel forces from in front.
A sense of impending reorganization hung over the office all autumn.
Nothing focuses a team like an impending audit.

impenetrable.definition: impossible to pass through or understand
sentences: The prose was impenetrable, which some reviewers mistook for depth.
The hedge was impenetrable to everything except the neighbor's cat.
One careless email imperiled a negotiation that had taken two years.
Cutting the inspections imperiled everyone and saved almost nothing.
An imperious wave sent the waiter across the room and the guests into silence.
Imperious manners work exactly as long as the authority behind them lasts.
The clay layer is impermeable, which is why the reservoir holds at all.
He was impermeable to advice from anyone paid less than he was.
The impertinent question was the only one worth answering.
Impertinent originally meant simply irrelevant, and rudeness attached itself later.
The imperturbable clerk processed the complaint, the shouting, and the apology identically.
Imperturbable is not the same as uncaring, though it is often mistaken for it.
He is impervious to criticism, which is a strength for a novelist and a flaw in a manager.
The coating is impervious to salt water and, apparently, to seagulls.
An impetuous resignation over lunch became a two-year legal matter.
Impetuous in youth and cautious in office is the usual sequence.

impetus.definition: a force that drives something forward
sentences: The scandal gave the reform an impetus that ten years of argument had not.
The impetus faded within a year and the committee met on.
He was charged with impiety, which in Athens covered almost any inconvenient question.
There is a mild impiety in laughing at your own field, and it is usually healthy.

impious.definition: showing no respect for the sacred
sentences: The impious joke was cut from the broadcast and circulated widely regardless.
An impious remark in the wrong century could cost a great deal more than a job.
An implacable creditor pursued the estate for nineteen years.
Time is implacable, which is the entire subject of most poetry.
The alibi was implausible and, inconveniently for the prosecution, true.
Real life is full of implausible coincidences that no editor would permit.
The receipts implicated three people who had insisted they never met.
He implicated himself by explaining something nobody had asked about.
The implication of the memo was clear and its wording was carefully not.
Consider the implications before congratulating yourself on the finding.
The implicit assumption was that someone else would do the checking.
She had implicit trust in her editor, which he had earned over twenty years.
The company imploded in six weeks, taking four suppliers with it.
Buildings are imploded on purpose so they fall on their own footprint.
It was impolitic to mention the audit at the retirement dinner.
Impolitic honesty ends more careers than dishonesty does.
The forecast handles the numbers and ignores the imponderables entirely.
Weather, mood, and traffic are the three imponderables of any launch day.
The importunate emails arrived nightly until somebody finally answered.
An importunate request eventually gets what a reasonable one could not.
He importuned the committee weekly until it created a rule about him.
Importuned by both sides, she published the data and satisfied neither.
The imposed deadline was met and the imposed method was quietly abandoned.
Order imposed from outside lasts exactly as long as the imposing.
The imposing entrance hall led to nine very small offices.
He was physically imposing and, in argument, entirely harmless.
Staying an extra hour was framed as a favor and functioned as an imposition.
The imposition of the levy was announced on a Friday afternoon, as always.

imposture.definition: the act of deceiving by pretending to be someone else
sentences: The imposture lasted eleven years and included two published papers.
An imposture is undone by one person who actually knows the field.
He muttered an imprecation at the printer and, briefly, felt better.
The letter ended with an imprecation that the lawyers advised removing.

impregnable.definition: unable to be captured or broken into
sentences: The impregnable fortress fell to a bribe rather than a siege.
His argument seemed impregnable until somebody checked the first citation.

improbable.definition: unlikely to be true or happen
sentences: An improbable sequence of small errors produced a completely predictable disaster.
Improbable things happen constantly, because there are so many of them available.

improvident.definition: failing to plan for the future
sentences: Improvident spending in the good years made the bad ones unsurvivable.
The improvident grasshopper is the villain of a fable written by ants.
When the projector died she improvised with a whiteboard and did better.
Improvising well requires knowing the material better than reading it would.

imprudence.definition: lack of care or good judgment
sentences: The imprudence was not the investment but the failure to read anything about it.
Youthful imprudence is forgiven; the same act at fifty is called character.
It was imprudent to sign before the survey and expensive to discover why.
An imprudent remark in a small town outlives the person who made it.
The impudent reply got him fired and quoted approvingly for a decade.
Impudent children grow into either comedians or defendants.

impugn.definition: to attack as false or questionable
sentences: He impugned her motives rather than address a single one of her figures.
To impugn a witness is a strategy; to refute one is an argument.
They dumped waste with impunity for eleven years and a fine of nine thousand.
Impunity is not the absence of rules but the absence of enforcement.

impute.definition: to attribute a fault or quality to
sentences: Never impute malice where a missed email will do.
The court declined to impute knowledge to a director who had signed the page.
An inadvertent copy-and-paste sent the salary list to the whole company.
Inadvertent harm still requires an apology, however sincere the surprise.
The panel discussion achieved a level of inanity rare even for conferences.
The inanity of the slogan was its greatest commercial strength.
He was inarticulate in meetings and devastating on paper.
Inarticulate rage is the hardest kind to answer or to help.
An inborn resistance to the disease protects about one person in three hundred.
Nothing about the talent was inborn; the willingness to practice may have been.
Her incandescent performance carried a production that was otherwise a shambles.
He was incandescent with rage, which was more informative than his usual calm.
Macbeth imagines the seas turned incarnadine, which is Shakespeare showing off.
The incarnadine sky at sunset made everyone stop and take the same photograph.
The incendiary speech was delivered to two hundred people and read by four million.
An incendiary device burns; an incendiary remark spreads faster.
The dismissal of the complaint incensed a group that had been merely annoyed.
One word in the second paragraph incensed the entire readership.
The incentive scheme rewarded speed and produced, predictably, a great deal of rework.
People respond to incentives, including the ones you did not intend to create.
The incessant drilling next door made working from home a theoretical option.
Incessant complaint achieves less than one well-timed letter.

inchoate.definition: just begun and not fully formed
sentences: The movement was inchoate: real anger, no leadership, and three competing hashtags.
An inchoate idea should not be judged by the standards of a finished one.
The incidental costs exceeded the main budget line by a factor of two.
An incidental detail in the footnote turned out to be the actual story.
Incipient cracks in the coalition were visible to everyone except the coalition.
Incipient panic in a crowd is quieter than you expect.
Her incisive summary reduced a three-hour argument to one printable sentence.
Incisive means cutting: it removes what does not matter.
The match was abandoned due to inclement weather and a flooded car park.
Inclement conditions revealed which of the tents had been tested.
I am inclined to agree, which is as close to a yes as he ever came.
She was inclined to caution and, on this occasion, spectacularly wasn't.
The price is inclusive, which is why the total surprised nobody at checkout.
An inclusive process takes longer and produces decisions that survive.

inconclusive.definition: not leading to a definite result
sentences: The tests were inconclusive, which the headline reported as a discovery.
Two inconclusive studies do not add up to one conclusive one.

incongruity.definition: a lack of harmony or fit
sentences: The incongruity of a chandelier in a garden shed was the whole joke.
Comedy is largely engineered incongruity delivered with a straight face.
His cheerful tie was incongruous at a hearing about mass redundancy.
The incongruous glass extension is either the building's ruin or its rescue.
The change looked inconsequential and altered every downstream calculation.
Meetings expand to fill the time with inconsequential detail.
The inconstancy of the funding made planning beyond a year impossible.
He was accused of inconstancy by people who had changed their minds twice as often.
The video evidence was incontrovertible and the denial continued anyway.
Very little is incontrovertible; a great deal is merely inconvenient to controvert.

incorporate.definition: to include as part of a whole
sentences: The final draft incorporated three objections and ignored the fourth entirely.
The design incorporates the old wall, which was cheaper than removing it.
He is an incorrigible optimist, which has cost him money and saved his health.
The word literally means uncorrectable, which teachers use fondly and courts use plainly.
The incredulous silence lasted long enough for him to repeat the number.
Incredulous is the listener; incredible is the claim.

incubation.definition: a period of development before emergence
sentences: The incubation of the idea took four years and its execution took six weeks.
The incubation period explains why the outbreak was invisible until it was everywhere.
The school inculcated punctuality so thoroughly that alumni arrive early to funerals.
Inculcate comes from stamping with the heel, which is how repetition feels.
The incumbent lost to a challenger who had campaigned for eleven months.
It is incumbent on the author to check what the footnote actually says.
She remained indebted to a teacher who never learned what she had done.
The company was indebted to three banks and loyal to none.
It was thought indecorous to celebrate before the results were confirmed.
The indecorous joke was cut from the speech and told in the bar.
The indefatigable volunteer answered letters for thirty years without pay.
Indefatigable means literally not able to be tired out, which few people qualify for.

indemnify.definition: to compensate for loss or protect from liability
sentences: The contract indemnified the supplier against everything except doing the job badly.
He was indemnified for the loss and never for the inconvenience.
The painting is of indeterminate date, which lowered the price and raised the interest.
Sentenced for an indeterminate period is a phrase that should alarm everybody.

indication.definition: a sign or piece of evidence
sentences: There was no indication of trouble until the third quarter, when there was nothing else.
An early indication is not a conclusion, though headlines disagree.

indict.definition: to formally charge with a crime
sentences: A grand jury would indict a ham sandwich, as the saying goes.
The report does not indict individuals; it indicts a system that produced them.

indictment.definition: a formal charge; a damning criticism
sentences: The waiting list is an indictment of a decade of decisions, not of any one nurse.
The indictment ran ninety pages and rested on a single spreadsheet.
Public indifference killed the proposal more efficiently than opposition would have.
The opposite of love is indifference, which requires no maintenance at all.
The service was indifferent and the food was worse, which the review said politely.
He was indifferent to praise and unusually sensitive to being ignored.
He died in indigence, and three museums now compete for his sketches.
Indigence is poverty severe enough to require someone else's decision.
The indigenous oak supports six hundred species; the imported ornamental supports four.
Indigenous knowledge of the coast predates every map of it.
Free legal representation exists for indigent defendants and is funded like an afterthought.
The indigent scholar dined on invitations for two years.
He was indignant about the accusation and specific about nothing else.
Indignant letters to the editor are the most reliable free content in publishing.
Public indignation lasted four days and changed one line of the policy.
Righteous indignation is the most enjoyable emotion and the least useful.
Indiscriminate cuts removed the waste and the two people who understood the system.
Indiscriminate praise is worth exactly as much as indiscriminate criticism.
The indispensable colleague went on leave and the department discovered it was true.
Graveyards are full of indispensable people, as the French say.
He indited a letter of complaint that took three days and was never sent.
Indite is to write; indict is to charge. They are pronounced identically, which is cruel.
An indolent summer produced nothing but a suntan and one very good idea.
He was indolent about everything except the one hobby he pursued fanatically.
Her indomitable insistence outlasted four ministers and won the inquiry.
Indomitable spirit is what we call stubbornness once it succeeds.
The industrious apprentice outlasted three clever ones.
Industrious is not the same as productive, as many long days demonstrate.

ineffable.definition: too great to be expressed in words
sentences: He described the ineffable for two pages, which rather undercut the claim.
The ineffable quality of the performance was, by definition, missing from every review.
The ineluctable arithmetic of the pension fund defeated every clever proposal.
Ineluctable means you cannot wrestle your way out, which is the literal root.
The inept cover-up drew more attention than the original error would have.
He was inept at small talk and formidable in a crisis.
The inequity was measurable, documented, and defended as tradition.
Inequity is unfairness; iniquity is wickedness. A single letter and a moral world apart.
He argued for the inerrancy of the text and against reading it closely.
Nobody has ever claimed inerrancy for a timetable, which shows some sense.
The committee was inert for two years and then, alarmingly, decisive.
Argon is inert, which is why it is used to protect things from air.
The inexorable rise of the water made the argument about drainage academic.
Inexorable means unmoved by pleading, which describes both glaciers and deadlines.
No system is infallible, and the ones described as such fail most spectacularly.
His infallible method worked twice and was retired quietly after the third attempt.
The infelicitous phrase in the press release cost a week of clarification.
An infelicitous choice of venue put the grief counselors next to the bar.
From the silence she inferred that the decision had already been made.
The speaker implies; the listener infers. Swapping them is the commonest error in English.
Moths infested the archive and ate exactly the box that mattered.
The comment section was infested with accounts created that morning.
Inflammable and flammable mean the same thing, which has caused actual fires.
The inflammable mood in the hall needed only one careless sentence.
The inflammatory headline was corrected on page nineteen a week later.
Inflammatory language in a crowded room is a physical act, not a verbal one.

inform.definition: to give shape to; to tell
sentences: A deep reading of the archives informs every page of the book without being visible.
Nobody informed the night staff, who discovered the closure on the door.
The ingenious solution used two paperclips and one insight nobody else had.
Ingenious is inventive; ingenuous is innocent. The two get swapped constantly.
She was cast as the ingenue at nineteen and refused the part at twenty.
The ingenue role has ruined more careers than it has launched.
Wartime ingenuity built a working radio from a razor blade and a pencil.
Ingenuity is what a small budget produces and a large one buries.
Her ingenuous question about the accounts emptied the room.
An ingenuous manner is the most effective disguise available, which is why it is suspected.

ingrained.definition: deeply fixed and hard to change
sentences: Ingrained habits survived the reorganization, the merger, and the motivational posters.
The stain was ingrained, as was the argument about who caused it.
He called them ingrates for not thanking him for a favor nobody had requested.
Every benefactor eventually suspects the world is full of ingrates.
He ingratiated himself with the board and never once spoke to the staff.
Ingratiating behavior is obvious to everyone except its intended target.

inherent.definition: existing as an essential part of something
sentences: The risk is inherent in the design and cannot be trained away.
Inherent limitations are the ones that survive every version of the plan.
Fear of looking foolish inhibits more questions than ignorance does.
The drug inhibits an enzyme, which sounds modest and changes everything downstream.
Constant interruption is inimical to the kind of thought the job requires.
The climate is inimical to olives and generous to everything else.
His inimitable style was imitated by four hundred writers, none successfully.
The inimitable thing about her lectures was that nobody left.
The iniquitous tax fell hardest on those least able to pay and stayed for forty years.
An iniquitous system rarely needs iniquitous individuals to operate it.
The pamphlet catalogued the iniquities of the mill and was banned within a month.
Iniquity is wickedness; inequity is unfairness. Both were present.
Nobody had an inkling of the resignation until the email arrived at seven.
She had an inkling in March and confirmation in September.
An innate sense of direction is mostly a well-practiced one.
The debate over what is innate has outlasted every generation of evidence.
The innocuous-looking clause let either party walk away without penalty.
An innocuous question at the right moment can end a career.
The fire alarm chose an inopportune moment during the marriage proposal.
An inopportune truth is still a truth, told badly.
An inordinate amount of the meeting concerned the biscuits.
He took inordinate pride in a hedge that took eleven years to grow.

inquest.definition: an official inquiry, especially into a death
sentences: The inquest found systemic failure and named nobody, as inquests do.
After the defeat came the inquest, which lasted longer than the season.
An inquisitive child asks the question the adults have agreed to leave alone.
Inquisitive is a compliment right up until it becomes a complaint.
His inscrutable expression during the negotiation was worth several million.
The rules were inscrutable, which was either incompetence or design.
Insensate rage broke a window and solved nothing.
The machinery grinds on, insensate, whatever the quarterly report says.
He was insensible to the offense he had caused and cheerfully repeated it.
By the third hour the audience was insensible to any further statistics.

insidious.definition: harmful in a gradual, hidden way
sentences: The most insidious errors are the ones that produce plausible results.
Insidious comes from ambush: the harm is waiting rather than charging.

insinuate.definition: to suggest slyly; to work in gradually
sentences: He insinuated that the results were convenient and refused to say so plainly.
She insinuated herself into the committee by volunteering for the worst subcommittee.
The insipid sequel kept the cast and lost whatever had made the first one work.
Insipid means without flavor, which applies to soup and to prose.
She insisted on seeing the raw data and found the error in twenty minutes.
He insisted he was calm, at volume.
The insolence of the reply was noted by everyone and punished by nobody.
Insolence from the powerless is bravery; from the powerful it is something else.
His insolent shrug ended a conversation that had been going quite well.
The insolent letter was framed by its recipient, which was the best possible answer.
The firm was insolvent for eleven months before anyone was legally required to say so.
Insolvent means the arithmetic has stopped working, whatever the confidence says.
He accepted the verdict with an insouciance that infuriated the prosecution.
Insouciance is charming in a friend and terrifying in a pilot.
The lecture inspired four students and irritated the other two hundred.
Inspire means to breathe in, which is a fair description of what a good idea feels like.
In this instance the rule was applied; in the four before it, it was not.
One instance is an anecdote; forty is a pattern.

institute.definition: to establish or set in motion
sentences: They instituted proceedings on a Friday, which delayed everything by a weekend.
The policy instituted in 1974 was reviewed for the first time in 2009.
He was insufferable after the promotion and, oddly, delightful before it.
The insufferable heat emptied the office by two o'clock.
The insular department cited only itself for a decade.
Insular literally means island-like, which is exactly the mental geography.
The insularity of the profession is its greatest defense and its permanent weakness.
